title: Pride and Prejudice - Chapter II
author: Jane Austen
description: Mr. Bennet reveals he has already visited Mr. Bingley, surprising his family after days of teasing. The chapter highlights the social maneuvers of the Bennet household and the contrasting personalities of the family members.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Bennet's secret visit to Bingley reveals that despite his sarcastic detachment, he is actively engaged in securing his daughters' future. His teasing serves as a psychological buffer against his wife's frantic social climbing.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: earliest of those who waited on Mr. Bingley.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mrs. Bennet's dismissal of Mrs. Long exposes the competitive nature of the marriage market. Her suspicion that Mrs. Long will prioritize her own nieces reflects the zero-sum game of Regency courtship.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: She is a selfish, hypocritical woman, and I have no opinion of her.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Kitty’s coughing acts as a physical manifestation of domestic tension. Mr. Bennet’s remark about her lack of 'discretion' in timing her coughs is a classic example of his tendency to treat family behavior as a theatrical performance.

Mr. Bennet's mock-praise of his wife's 'circumspection' highlights the absurdity of Regency introductory rites. He points out that social 'knowing' is often superficial, regardless of the time spent together.

Mary is defined by her desire for intellectual status, yet she lacks the 'quickness' of Elizabeth. Her inability to find something 'sensible' to say emphasizes her role as a comic foil to the more naturally witty sisters.

The rapid shift in Mrs. Bennet's attitude from sickness of Mr. Bingley to rapturous joy illustrates her volatile and singular focus. Her claim that she 'expected' it all along is a defense mechanism for her social ego.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: what she had expected all the while.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Lydia’s boast about her height being a substitute for age-related social standing foreshadows her impulsive and reckless nature. She views the social world with a crude, physical confidence that lacks Elizabeth's nuance.
